segments.caption: A chips brand says every packet has 50 grams. You weigh 25 packets, and the average is only 48 grams.
Are they cheating, or is it just normal variation? Hypothesis testing decides.
Here's the textbook definition, the one to use in interviews.
Hypothesis testing is a statistical method that uses sample data to decide between two competing claims about a population: the null hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis.
In plain words: is the pattern in the data real, or just chance?
The null hypothesis, H0, says nothing special is going on: the packets really average 50 grams.
The alternative, H1, says something is going on: they average less.
We always start by assuming the null is true.
Every test has this pair.
A coin: fair, or biased. A website button: no change, or more clicks.
A new teaching method: no difference, or higher scores.
It's like a courtroom: innocent until proven guilty.
We reject the null only with strong evidence. Not enough evidence means not guilty, which is not the same as innocent.
A test has four steps.
One: state the two hypotheses. Two: pick a significance level, usually 5%.
Three: calculate the p-value.
If the packets really averaged 50 grams, an average this low would happen only about 1% of the time.
Four: decide. 1% is below 5%, so we reject the null. The packets really are underfilled.
Now suppose the average had been 49.5 grams.
That happens about 27% of the time by chance, so we fail to reject the null.
That doesn't prove the packets are full. There's just not enough evidence.
One more example: a coin lands heads 9 times out of 10.
If the coin were fair, 9 or more heads would happen only about 1% of the time.
Below 5%, so we reject the null. The coin is probably biased.
So remember: assume nothing special is going on, collect data,
and reject that assumption only when the data would be really surprising.
Quick quiz!
A school claims its new teaching method raises test scores.
What is the null hypothesis?
No change!
The null always says: no effect, no difference. The school must bring enough evidence to reject it.
Next: how surprising is the data? The p-value.
Follow for data science made simple!
